2611.18860.abstract: We need spectroscopic imaging at sub-millimetre wavelengths to answer fundamental questions about the origins of our universe, structure formation and galaxy evolution. Often, there are steep trade-offs between the number of detectors and their spectral resolving power in completing such 3D surveys. Novel astrophotonics technologies, such as the Superconducting On-Chip Fourier Transform Spectrometer (SOFTS), are underway to break instrumentation barriers and enable the packing of a focal-plane array with many high spectral resolution submillimeter detectors. Here, we summarize recent advances in SOFTS development, focusing on potential spectroscopic resolution and packing density within a focal plane array.

2611.18943.abstract: The Affordable Multiple-Aperture Spectroscopy Explorer (AMASE) project aims to enable high-resolution spectroscopy of ionised gas in galaxies. However, fabricating ultra- dense fibre bundles with micrometre-level precision presents significant challenges. We detail a fabrication process that combines precision machining, stress-reducing handling, and iterative polishing. Although the final prototype did not meet the optical performance targets, our methods reduced manual labour, improved reproducibility, and identified critical failure modes, providing essential information for future astrophotonic instrument designs.

2611.18968.abstract: Radio antennas are often used to form arrays, such as phased arrays and interferometer arrays. For most applications the beam patterns of these instruments must be accurately known. For phased arrays the array patterns are formed by coherently adding the embedded element patterns (EEPs) of the individual antennas in the array. For interferometers, the fundamental measurement is of visibilities, which depend on the products of pairs of EEPs. Unfortunately, in either case, for closely-spaced arrays, the EEPs can be distorted by mutual coupling between the antennas and can be very different from the isolated element patterns (IEPs), measured when the antennas are far apart. Mutual coupling is characterized by the scattering parameters for the array. Full-wave electromagnetic simulations can simulate the EEPs, including mutual coupling effects, but these simulations can be computationally expensive and require accurate knowledge of the design of the array elements, their placement, and the environment in which they are deployed. Directly measuring either the EEPs or the array patterns for instruments in the field is often impractical as well. In this paper we show that in cases where the scattering parameters between array elements can be measured, they can be used to infer the array patterns of a phased array. We demonstrate the training of a deep neural network to simulate array patterns when given: the design of the antennas, the locations of the antennas, the frequency of operation, and measurements of the scattering parameters of the array. As a demonstration for a simple model, we apply this approach to the simulation of the array patterns for a small phased array of three dipole antennas and evaluate the sensitivity of this procedure to uncertainties in measurements of the antenna positions and scattering parameters.

2611.19579.abstract: Existing calendars, in particular the Gregorian calendar, have a complex structure which requires constant adjustment in the form of leap days and leap seconds in order to remain synchronized to the position of a planet in the Solar System. In addition, mean solar days can deviate up to 16 minutes from true solar days on Earth. On other planets, this discrepancy can be far greater: on Mars, it can be up to 51 minutes. Numerous Martian proposals ranging from Aitken (1936) to Gangale (1986) to Silin (2025) mimic the Gregorian calendar and do not address these issues. Moreover, many do not include a system for telling the time of day, or stretch the second beyond the standard SI second. This paper proposes a calendar mechanism that uses years and days with a variable duration, in order to accurately represent true solar years and days. In this mechanism, time of day is expressed as a proportion, rather than a number of fixed units, such as hours and minutes. This results in a simple and consistent structure that can universally be applied to any planet, moon or space station with a human presence. Furthermore, it allows analog missions on Earth to use the same calendar mechanism as future missions in space. This paper will outline the principles and details of this mechanism, using Earth and Mars as illustrative examples. Also discussed is the implementation of the mechanism on actual computers, which have a Unix time system clock based on discrete milliseconds.

2611.19734.abstract: We document the data reduction, reconstruction choices, and available uncertainty propagation underlying fifteen PHAROS stellar spectral energy distributions from 0.5 to 5000 nm. A catalogue timeline and a practical FITS guide introduce the available products, their column and extension conventions, and examples of reading, integration, and uncertainty display. Shared methods are presented once, including flux geometry, support-aware integration, X-ray likelihoods, the 2025 X/EUV luminosity relation, intrinsic Ly$\alpha$ inference, airglow treatment, spectral junctions, and covariance-aware resampling. Target sections record the adopted observations and alternatives, including spatially separated binary components, unresolved system-level EUV measurements, direct EUVE constraints, optical stellar-twin transfer, and literature-anchored cases where new spectral inference is unsupported. The distinction between native measurement errors, conditional model intervals, empirical predictive scatter, and physical-method sensitivity is maintained. Signed measurements and nonnegative irradiation products are distinguished. Each target section concludes with the final nominal spectrum and its available uncertainty bounds on common axes. This library provides the detailed provenance and interpretation needed to accompany the catalogue paper and its machine-readable products.

2611.20300.abstract: In recent years, the traditional Lomb--Scargle periodogram, relying on least-squares fitting of a sinusoid to data with a known mean, has been mostly superseded by its floating-mean extension---the generalized Lomb--Scargle periodogram---due to the superior robustness and accuracy of the latter. While further generalization to higher-degree trigonometric polynomials (known as the multiharmonic analysis of variance and the fast $\chi^2$ periodogram) has been known for decades, its usage remains relatively uncommon, mostly due to its significantly higher computational cost. Here we present a technique reducing the computational complexity of such an extension by combining a Toeplitz formulation of the system of normal equations with non-uniform fast Fourier transforms, coupled with condition-number monitoring to protect against numerical instability. When modified for practical efficiency rather than asymptotic computational complexity, our approach reaches speed-ups exceeding an order of magnitude over current state-of-the-art implementations across a wide range of hyperparameters when evaluated on multithreaded systems, while matching or exceeding their accuracy. Additionally, we provide a reference implementation used for benchmarking, along with the code used to generate the results presented in this work.

2611.20343.abstract: We have developed high-resolution electroformed nickel X-ray telescope mirrors by extending precision mirror-fabrication techniques developed for synchrotron X-ray microscopy to space astronomy. Our previous study identified axial figure errors of a replicated mirror as one of the factors limiting its X-ray angular resolution. In the present study, we fabricated a new mirror using a substantially improved mandrel and directly compared the two-dimensional figure errors of the mandrels and replicated inner mirror surfaces for both the previous and new mandrel--mirror pairs. This comparison reveals how contributions to the final mirror figure errors changed with improved mandrel accuracy. For the previous mirror, the mandrel and mirror showed a strong spatial correlation in their figure errors, indicating that a substantial component of the mirror figure pattern was inherited from the mandrel. In contrast, after improving the mandrel figure, the new mirror exhibited a weaker mandrel--mirror spatial correlation, while the residual figure deviations arising between the mandrel and final mirror became comparable in magnitude to the residual mandrel figure errors. The improved mandrel reduced the central 68% widths, W68, of the axial slope error distribution from 3.3 to 1.6 arcsec for the paraboloidal surface and from 5.0 to 1.1 arcsec for the hyperboloidal surface. Correspondingly, the mirror values improved from 4.6 to 2.4 arcsec and from 12.4 to 2.0 arcsec, respectively. X-ray measurements at 12 keV yielded local half power diameters (HPDs) of approximately 7--17 arcsec and a full-aperture HPD of 8.5 arcsec. The newly fabricated mirror was adopted for the soft X-ray telescope of the fifth Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager (FOXSI-5) sounding rocket flight and was successfully flown in May 2026.

2611.20357.abstract: We investigate the demographic evolution of the Japanese astronomy and astrophysics publication community during 1996-2025 using bibliometric data from 23,274 publications in major journals in the field. The number of active Japan-affiliated authors increased from approximately 600 in the late 1990s to more than 2,000 by the early 2020s, while annual publication output reached approximately 1,400 by 2025. Participation was highly heterogeneous, with 46% of authors observed in only one publication year within the study period and a smaller core showing long observed participation periods. We define the Community Renewal Rate (CRR) as a community-level measure of renewal, calculated as the fraction of active authors not observed during a specified preceding interval. The 5-year CRR typically remained near one quarter of the active community, with annual values ranging from approximately 21% to 33%, indicating persistent renewal despite substantial community growth. An order-of-magnitude comparison suggests that newly entering students account for only part of the renewal-author population. The community therefore expanded while sustaining both continuity through authors with long observed participation periods and renewal through recurring changes in active membership.

2611.20418.abstract: A new epoch for direct visualisation of accretion dynamics near a black hole's event horizon began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (EHTC) synthesised an Earth-sized aperture with millimeter radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features, with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source. Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very-long baseline interferometry (VLBI) measurements, rendering interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms, and imaging hyperparameters. Here, we apply a newly-developed independent imaging algorithm to the M87* dataset, which is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image, and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with angular diameter 42.2 +/- 1.5 microarcseconds corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 +/- 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of ~20 deg from the approaching jet.

2611.20520.abstract: Context. The direct detection and atmospheric characterization of terrestrial exoplanets has been highlighted as a key science focus by the US ASTRO2020 Decadal survey and the ESA Voyage 2050 plan. This will require a new generation of telescope which is able to meet the contrast requirements necessary to image a planet many orders of magnitude fainter than its host star - a technological feat which currently limits our observation capabilities. In the mid-infrared, the most viable solution has been shown to be a formation-flying nulling space interferometer. Aims. In this work, we present the initial prototype for an inter-spacecraft metrology system. This system is a sub-system of the Pyxis/SEIRIOS interferometer, a formation-flying interferometer which serves as a technology demonstrator for the LIFE mission. Methods. We have designed a multi-stage metrology system using three interferometric measurement techniques, covering varying distance resolution ranges. Digital Interferometric (DI) ranging provides the coarsest measurement, while a differential phase read-out provides sub-nm precision. Multi-wavelength interferometry is employed to overcome the phase ambiguity associated with the differential phase readout. Results. A single-wavelength electronic noise floor below 20 pm RMS over 10 s was measured by applying a common photodetector signal to both readout channels, a factor of 28 below the 560 pm requirement. For the multi-wavelength readout, the obtained electronic noise RMS was 556 nm at 10 second integration, decreasing to 200 nm below 3 second integration. The full optical measurement in laboratory air is currently limited by environmental path fluctuations. Conclusions. We demonstrate an initial prototype system for precision ranging between satellites for formation-flying nulling interferometers.

2611.21353.abstract: The reduced speed of light approximation (RSLA) is a common approach in radiation-hydrodynamic (RHD) simulations of non-relativistic systems where the gas speed $v_{\rm gas} \ll c$. In the RSLA one eases the severe time step constraint imposed by the speed of light $c$ by replacing it with a reduced value $\hat{c}$ chosen so that $v_{\rm gas} \ll \hat{c} \ll c$. This approach works well in flows with low or moderate optical depth, but fails in optically thick media, where it makes thermal relaxation too slow and gives incorrect RHD wave modes. Here we propose an Adaptive Reduced Speed of Light Approximation (ARSA) that removes these problems by replacing the global speed reduction factor $\phi_0 \equiv \hat{c}/c$ with a local, cell-by-cell reduction factor $\phi$ derived from a von Neumann stability analysis of the implicit-explicit update used by modern two-moment RHD codes. The resulting limiter has no tunable parameters, can be computed using only local operations, and improves on the classic RSLA by allowing $\phi \to 1$ in cells where a reduced speed of light is not required because the exchange with the gas damps unstable modes, allowing recovery of the correct thermal relaxation and wave-damping rates in highly-opaque regions. We compare ARSA to the classic RSLA in a range of standard RHD test problems, and show that in opaque regions where gas holds most of the heat capacity the ARSA is much more accurate than the RSLA at the same time step, or that it can achieve the same accuracy as the RSLA with up to 100 times fewer time steps. However, gains are limited in regions where radiation holds a large share of the heat capacity, as it does in some astrophysical systems.

2611.21510.abstract: Gaia has observed every detected source on the sky 50 to 100 times, each time through a window of about 1 by 2 arcseconds at a different scan angle. The resulting one-dimensional flux profiles to be released in Gaia DR4 encode the two-dimensional arrangement of nearby point sources at ~0.1 arcsecond resolution. Repeated observations also constrain their relative motion. We present a method to model the scene with a mixture of moving point sources. Complementing Gaia DPAC's source-environment reconstruction, our approach focuses on close, blended companions and models their relative motion. We first fit each window with a few point sources and obtain their along-scan positions. We then triangulate these positions from different scan angles to identify candidate sources on the sky. A joint forward model of all windows measures positions, fluxes, relative proper motions, and parallax differences, even for blended components. In simulations, we recover companions at separations smaller than the instrumental profile width. For a moving companion at ~75 mas separation with a flux ratio of ~0.2, we obtain a separation precision of ~0.1 mas and a relative proper-motion precision of ~0.1 mas/yr per component, even in a scene contaminated by a third source. These precisions assume a known instrumental profile and independent Gaussian noise. We also recover differential parallax for a chance-aligned source. Modeling nearby contaminants prevents significant biases. With a Gaia-like instrumental profile, sampling and scan law, we show a sensitivity of ~5 mag in contrast at separations of 50-150 mas, and we discuss its dependence on the color term of Gaia's line-spread function. The method could extend the census of close companions and provide relative astrometry, and so dynamical information, along short orbital arcs. External measurements could also guide retrospective searches in Gaia's windows.

2611.18584.title: Powering the Space Elevator

figures.caption: Figure 2.1:  This graph shows the ratio of the apparent gravitational acceleration felt by a climber at any altitude to the acceleration of gravity at the surface of the Earth. The apparent gravity is not just the force of gravity caused by the mass of Earth, but it also accounts for the reduction in apparent weight of the climber the higher it goes caused by the rotation of the Earth. The graph stops at GEO because above GEO it does not take external power to climb toward the Apex. 2611.18584.abstract: Powering the Space Elevator is a report on the work of an International Space Elevator Consortium study group tasked with determining the technology options for delivering power to the climbers on the space elevator at any altitude above Earth. The book covers options such as laser power beaming, microwave beaming, a solar-powered climber, and delivering power through the electrical conductivity of the tether. This report starts with the reference conceptual design of a climber from the 2023 study report, "The Climber/Tether Interface of the Space Elevator," and adds features to the climber that allow it to ascend or descend the elevator tether. 2611.18688.abstract: For low background experiments, prediction of the background from radioactivity in detector components is of critical importance. Radioassays are often conducted on small samples or individual parts, which may be subject to differences in production or handling resulting in a part-to-part variation. This part-to-part variation can have an impact on the total activity and is not presently captured by the averaging methods used to evaluate radioassays. We propose a new method for the averaging of radioassays to incorporate this part-to-part variation into predictions of the total activity of parts. We also consider how to add component activities based on assays for component groups that are simulated as a single entity.

2611.18912.abstract: The excellent infrared sensitivity of JWST allows direct imaging of young low-mass (below $\sim1$ M$_{\text{Jup}}$) giant planets for the first time, with several JWST programs being carried out for this purpose. However, the detection sensitivity of these observations crucially depends on subtracting the residual light of the host star to reveal faint astrophysical signals. This requires high quality observations of reference stars to build an empirical starlight model. Here we present a homogeneously processed reference star library of targets observed with programs GO 4050, GO 5835 and SURVEY 6005, which enable PSF subtraction via reference star differential imaging. These observations were taken with the MASK335R coronagraph mask and in dual-filter F444W/F200W mode. Our library consists of 247 observations (counting both filters separately) of 100 different stars of spectral types mostly F to M, with a total of 1110 individual integrations. We explore the PSF subtraction hyper-parameters with the KLIP algorithm (Soummer et al. 2012) that maximize sensitivity, and we show the performance of our library compared to and in addition to contemporaneous reference observations. We show that our library improves sensitivity at close separations in most tested cases, with improvement factors from $\sim1.3$ to $\sim2$ at some separations. As practical recommendations, we find that our library is best used as a complement to contemporaneous reference observations to further improve sensitivity, since in all our experiments contemporaneous references are needed for best sensitivity. We make the PSF library publicly available for the high-contrast imaging community.

2611.19015.abstract: Kepler recorded several thousand dedicated sky-background pixels per detector output every 29.4 min from 2009 to 2013, an archive that we use to study comets. During 2010 April 14-21 a narrow band of excess light swept across the field at 1.46 deg/day. This feature is the ion tail of comet C/2009 K5 (McNaught), whose head passed just beyond the edge of the detector array. We trace the tail from 0.9 deg to ~13 deg from the nucleus at surface brightnesses of 26.7-30 mag/arcsec^2; its aberration implies a solar-wind speed of ~500-750 km/s. At 30-min cadence we follow a tail-disconnection event on 2010 April 17-19 whose timing and geometry are consistent with a flank encounter with a coronal mass ejection, although other triggers cannot be excluded. We then analyze all 21 known comets with perihelion distance q < 15 AU whose heads crossed the detectors, using photometry at the predicted head positions calibrated against displaced control tracks. Eight comets are detected, including C/2010 J4 (WISE) a few days before its discovery and two comets at 6.3-7.4 AU with one-sided streaks that we interpret as dust tails. The undetected comets give 3-sigma limits of typically Kp > 16.6-18.1 within 5 arcmin of the head. A blind shift-and-stack search for moving diffuse sources, roughly 50% complete at Kp ~ 15.5-16 for rates of 0.3-1 deg/day, recovers four known comets and finds no unknown ones. Animations show the K5 tail and comets C/2011 L3 and C/2010 J4 crossing the field.

2611.19400.abstract: Large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations rely on tabulated nuclear equations of state (EOSs), whose memory requirements can become a practical constraint in massively parallel calculations. We explore a compact alternative by replacing the tabulated thermodynamic mapping with a neural-network surrogate, using the Lattimer--Swesty EOS as a representative reference model. The surrogate directly predicts pressure, sound speed, and effective adiabatic index from $(\log \rho, \log e, Y_e)$ and accurately reconstructs the nonlinear thermodynamic structure of the EOS, including its behavior across phase-transition regions. It reproduces one-dimensional shock-tube solutions with hydrodynamic errors at the $\sim 10^{-3}$ level under different thermodynamic conditions and yields hydrostatic equilibrium configurations closely matching those obtained with the reference EOS. We find that smaller regression errors do not necessarily yield better hydrodynamic performance, demonstrating the importance of hydrodynamic validation in surrogate model selection. A compact network with only $\sim 10^4$ parameters retains this accuracy while reducing the memory required to store the EOS from $\sim 160$ MB to $\sim 100$ KB, corresponding to a reduction by a factor of $\sim 1500$. The surrogate also remains stable through collapse, bounce, shock formation, and post-bounce evolution in a one-dimensional adiabatic core-collapse calculation. These results demonstrate the potential of compact neural EOS surrogates for reducing memory requirements in large-scale core-collapse supernova simulations.

2611.19657.abstract: Kepler recorded several thousand dedicated sky-background pixels per detector output every 29.4 min from 2009 May to 2013 May while staring at a fixed 12-degree field at ecliptic latitude +65 degrees. From this archive we isolate a large-scale layer that measures brightness variations relative to an 8-day running median. This layer contains fluctuations of 0.02-0.1 electrons per second per pixel (about 1e-17 of the mean solar surface brightness) that sweep across the field in a day or less. Four lines of evidence show that these are sunlight Thomson-scattered by solar-wind electrons. (1) The sweeps propagate away from the Sun (84 percent within 45 degrees of the anti-solar direction; 25 percent expected by chance), and their direction follows the Sun through each quarter and across all 16 spacecraft rolls. (2) The field brightness correlates with the near-Earth (OMNI) proton density within a day of zero lag (r = 0.19, p < 1/150), but not with the energetic-proton flux. (3) Time-elongation maps show fronts moving outward at a median 15 degrees per day, as forward models of radially moving density structures predict. (4) The amplitude is about one third of a parameter-free Thomson-scattering prediction and varies by a factor of about 3 over the year, as predicted. Half of the scattered light comes from within 0.4-0.7 AU of the spacecraft. Fronts are strongest in slow wind. Kepler's background pixels thus provide a four-year, high-cadence, out-of-ecliptic record of solar-wind structure near 1 AU. Standard Kepler processing removes these signals, changing stellar light curves by less than about 1 ppm.

2611.19899.abstract: We present the current implementation of an automated framework developed within the Legacy Survey of Space and Time Dark Energy Science Collaboration (LSST DESC) for galaxy cluster cosmology, in preparation for the first LSST data releases of the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. The cluster cosmology pipeline integrates DESC-developed tools dedicated to galaxy/cluster catalog ingestion, cluster number count and weak lensing measurements, modeling, and parameter inference through posterior sampling, enabling reproducible end-to-end cluster cosmology analyses. We test and validate the pipeline using synthetic mock datasets and the LSST DESC cosmoDC2 simulation, performing a joint analysis of redMaPPer cluster abundance and stacked weak lensing profiles measured in bins of redshift and richness. We constrain two cosmological parameters, $\Omega_c$ and $\sigma_8$, along with six cluster mass-observable relation parameters. Our baseline analysis recovers the fiducial cosmoDC2 values of $\Omega_c$ and $\sigma_8$ within $0.51\sigma$ and $0.34\sigma$, respectively. We also showcase the flexibility of the overall pipeline by assessing the impact of fiducial cosmology and alternative modeling prescriptions on the parameter constraints. Lastly, we also discuss the current limitations of the pipeline and the developments needed for LSST data.

2611.19918.abstract: Periods with only one detector operating accounted for 13.3 percent of the third LIGO-Virgo observing run (O3) and 29.7 percent of the first part of the fourth observing run (O4a). We present the first dedicated single-detector implementation of the Summed Parallel Infinite Impulse Response (SPIIR) pipeline for binary neutron star (BNS) and neutron star-black hole (NSBH) merger searches. Our hybrid log-likelihood ratio combines signal-consistency models for non-Gaussian glitches with a profile likelihood ratio for the signal-to-noise ratio under a Gaussian-noise model. We calibrate the glitch model by source category and trigger-rate class. We assign false alarm rates (FARs) using the measured background from the same detector and analysis chunk, extrapolating its high-ranking tail. We check the FAR assignments by comparing observed and expected cumulative background counts for BNS in O3a and NSBH in O3b at LIGO Hanford (H1) and LIGO Livingston (L1). Using O3 data and the GWTC-3 injection set, we find that, at a threshold of one false alarm per two months, the BNS sensitive distances are $136.5^{+2.9}_{-3.0}$ Mpc in L1 and $120.2^{+3.1}_{-3.3}$ Mpc in H1. These central estimates are approximately 24 and 38 percent higher, respectively, than the GWTC-3 GstLAL values of $110.5^{+3.2}_{-3.4}$ Mpc and $87.2^{+3.6}_{-3.9}$ Mpc over the same data and injection parameter ranges. GstLAL provides the only published single-detector results in GWTC-3. For NSBH, SPIIR reaches $164.1^{+6.7}_{-7.3}$ Mpc in L1 and $134.9^{+6.3}_{-7.0}$ Mpc in H1, compared with $165.1^{+6.7}_{-7.3}$ Mpc and $156.0^{+5.9}_{-6.4}$ Mpc for GWTC-3 GstLAL, respectively. Targeted searches recover triggers associated with GW190425, GW200105_162426, and GW230529_181500 with assigned FARs below the same threshold.

2611.20004.abstract: We investigate superradiant cloud level transitions in stellar-mass black hole binaries with milli-Hertz and multiband gravitational-wave observations. Under the adopted cloud formation and survival conditions, the $\lvert322\rangle\rightarrow\lvert31-1\rangle$ fine transition can imprint phase corrections in the LISA band, while Bohr transitions occurring after the milli-Hertz band observation can be probed through shifts in the merger time. Modeling the coupled cloud-orbit evolution, we find that cloud depletion can begin before resonance and that ionization can advance rather than delay coalescence. For a representative nearby binary, a vacuum injection-recovery analysis yields a cloud-mass-fraction posterior concentrated at $M_c^i/M\lesssim10^{-6}$. Comparing the LISA-predicted coalescence time with a subsequent ground-based measurement provides a complementary test of later cloud evolution. These results motivate complementary searches for ultralight bosons with milli-Hertz and multiband gravitational-wave observations.

2611.20290.abstract: We tracked the large, geoeffective halo coronal mass ejection (CME) of 2025-May-31 across the very wide field of view of the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission, as a proof of concept for data-informed forecasting of CME arrival times at Earth. using simple point-and-click measurement of the front location as far as 47 degrees away from the Sun itself, we constrained an analytic "ludicrous ice-cream cone" geometric model with just three parameters: position angle, off-Earth-Sun angle, and propagation speed. We show that the model is sufficient to capture the bulk envelope of the CME, and also insufficient to capture the complexity of the CME's evolution. We generated simulated arrival-time forecasts for the CME by extrapolating the constant-velocity propagation to determine the time of impact with Earth. These "retro-forecasts" converged to within 30 +/- 15 minutes of the actual arrival time, 8 hours prior to arrival. The convergence was marked by a clear inflection point in the curve of predicted-arrival-time vs time-of-forecast. We conclude that continuous wide-field tracking is sufficiently powerful to enable even crude models to substantially improve arrival-time forecasting precision, and discuss future work required both to validate this single-event result and to extend it to more sophisticated analyses.

2611.20636.abstract: The $Gaia$ high-resolution spectroscopic observations using Radial Velocity Spectrometer offers a unique opportunity to study stellar Ca II infrared triplet (IRT) activity. A key step in estimating activity indices is subtracting the photospheric contribution. The canonical template-based method often fails because, for many stars, the observed line cores are deeper than the model predictions, which prevents valid activity measurements. In this work, we explore an alternative approach that constructs a baseline from less active stars as a function of effective temperature (and metallicity) to represent the photospheric contribution. Our results show that, for dwarf stars, compared with the canonical method, the baseline method not only yields far more objects with valid activity measurements, but also avoids many extremely low and unreliable values (e.g., log$R'_{\rm IRT} \lesssim -6$). The Ca II IRT activity indices derived from the baseline method correlate well with other activity proxies, confirming their reliability as activity indicators. Furthermore, they show a relation with stellar rotation, not only recovering the typical rotation--activity relation, but also revealing fine structures that may be associated with different regimes in gyrochronology. Our findings suggest that the baseline method can serve as a robust alternative for deriving accurate activity estimates, and will be particularly useful for obtaining activity indices for tens of millions of stars with the upcoming $Gaia$ Data Release 4.

2611.20754.abstract: Electron-recoil directionality can help distinguish solar-neutrino interactions from backgrounds and, together with recoil-energy measurements and three-dimensional tracking, enable neutrino-energy spectroscopy. We study the reconstruction of the initial direction of low-energy electron recoils in the CYGNO optical time-projection chamber, focusing on the 50 L LIME prototype and its high-granularity scientific CMOS (sCMOS) readout. A dedicated algorithm identifies the interaction point from the asymmetry of the track light distribution and estimates the recoil direction from the early portion of the ionization trail, before multiple scattering erases most of the directional information. The method is characterized with a detailed Monte Carlo simulation of electron recoils and detector response. Samples spanning 15 keV to 70 keV are used to optimize the algorithm parameters by minimizing the width of the reconstructed-minus-true projected-angle distribution. The projected angular response is modeled by two Gaussian components that account for its dependence on track inclination. The narrower component, associated with favorable projections approximately parallel to the Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) plane, has a width that improves from about $20^\circ$ near 20 keV to about $12^\circ$ at 60 keV. We also quantify the fraction of events in the correctly reconstructed angular core and discuss the dominant limitations of a camera-only two-dimensional measurement.

2611.20785.abstract: One of the key goals of planetary population studies is to achieve broad coverage of the parameter space, which is not yet fully represented by confirmed planets. This limitation can be mitigated by including planets that have been statistically validated through a vetting procedure, even if they are not fully confirmed. In preparation for the Ariel mission, a Mission Candidate Sample has been assembled, comprising both confirmed planets and several unvalidated candidates. In this context, we apply a vetting analysis to a selected subsample of these candidates. Our methodology is based on the TRICERATOPS tool, aimed at confirming the presence of transiting planets or ruling out false-positive scenarios. We applied TRICERATOPS to a sample of 318 targets drawn from the last three Ariel TESS Planet Candidates catalogues. The analysis includes evaluation of statistical probabilities, as well as checks on stellar binarity indicators such as the Renormalized Unit Weight Error (RUWE) and the IPD_frac_multi_peak values from Gaia Data Release 3. Our analysis validated 56 candidates as planets, identified 29 false positives, and classified 35 as likely planets. These results are intended to support the Ariel mission by providing a probabilistic priority ranking to guide follow-up observations and optimise targets for atmospheric characterisation studies.

2611.21175.abstract: Galactic Chemical Evolution (GCE) models connect stellar nucleosynthesis to observed abundance patterns, but their interpretation requires simultaneous parameter inference and comparison between competing stellar yield prescriptions. This remains challenging due to intractable likelihoods and growing dataset complexity. Using compass, a novel simulation-based inference framework, we perform, for the first time, amortized joint Bayesian model comparison and parameter inference for GCE models with intractable likelihoods within a unified architecture. Compass employs a conditional score-based diffusion model with a transformer architecture to learn both the posterior and likelihood directly from forward simulations, enabling efficient inference and likelihood-based ranking of competing nucleosynthetic yield sets. In controlled tests, compass identifies the generating yield set and recovers ground-truth parameters with accuracy comparable to existing simulation-based inference (SBI) methods, while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude. Applied to Milky Way data, the framework favors a hybrid NuGrid + IllustrisTNG yield prescription, confirmed by an independent classifier, and infers an initial mass function slope of $\alpha_{\rm IMF} = -2.65 \pm 0.02$ and a SN$_{\rm Ia}$ normalization of $\log(N_{\rm Ia}) = -2.81 \pm 0.02$, with a systematic spread of $\approx 0.3$ in $\alpha_{\rm IMF}$ between the best-ranked yield sets, consistent with independent constraints. The attention mechanism confirms that the inferred parameters are driven by physically meaningful abundance signatures. By unifying amortized parameter inference, Bayesian model comparison, and interpretability in a single probabilistic framework, compass provides a scalable approach for precision chemical evolution studies with current and forthcoming spectroscopic surveys.

2611.21323.abstract: The proposed decihertz gravitational-wave (GW) band $(\sim 10^{-2}-1\,\Hz)$ will observe the late inspiral of intermediate mass-ratio inspirals (IMRIs), binaries with mass ratios $10^2 \lesssim q \lesssim 10^4$ that assemble dynamically in dense stellar environments and are expected to retain measurable eccentricity. Search and parameter-estimation pipelines are predominantly built around circular templates, and we test this assumption. Using black-hole perturbation theory waveforms from \textsc{FastEMRIWaveforms} for a representative IMRI ($M=10^4\,\modot$, $q=100$, observed for its final $10\,\hr$), we compute fitting factors between eccentric signals and circular templates, maximizing over the template's total mass and mass ratio with a differential-evolution search, for the B-DECIGO, LGWA-Si, and IndIGO-D noise curves and a flat PSD. The mismatch grows with initial eccentricity $e_0$ and crosses the standard $3\%$ threshold at $e_0\simeq3\times10^{-2}$, well within the range allowed by the waveform model and expected from dynamical formation. The best-fitting circular templates also bias the total mass and mass ratio by several percent at $e_0=0.1$. Combining the mismatch with the signal-to-noise-dependent distinguishability criterion, we find that for a source at $1\,\mathrm{Gpc}$, eccentricities as small as $e_0\simeq5\times10^{-4}$ (B-DECIGO and IndIGO-D) and $5\times10^{-3}$ (LGWA-Si) are resolvable, one to two orders of magnitude below where detection efficiency degrades. The loss of match arises from the excitation of radial Teukolsky harmonics, which spread power into sidebands that circular templates cannot represent, and from the slower orbital decay of eccentric binaries at fixed initial semi-latus rectum. Robust detection and parameter estimation of IMRIs with DECIGO, LGWA, and IndIGO-D will require eccentric waveform models and template banks.
